chapters.title: Chapter 1: How Business Income Gets Taxed in India

lessons.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025: Tax Year, Key Terms and What Changed

body.text: The Income-tax Act, 2025 did not change how much tax you pay. It changed where the rules are written, what they are called and how they are numbered. Treat it as a new address for the same tax, not a new tax.

children.text: On 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 1961 stopped governing new income and the Income-tax Act, 2025 took over. Sixty-five years of amendments, provisos and exceptions had made the old law almost unreadable for anyone who was not a specialist. The rewrite cut the word count roughly in half, replaced dense prose with tables and formulae, and gave every provision a new number.
For a business owner, three things matter: the new vocabulary, the section numbers your team will actually quote, and the fact that your tax bill itself is unchanged.

stats.label: Sections
stats.context: Down from 819 effective sections in the 1961 Act

stats.label: Tables
stats.context: Up from 18, plus 46 formulae against 6 earlier

events.title: Bill introduced in Parliament
events.description: The rewrite followed a review in which the CBDT set up 22 sub-committees, one for each area of the old Act, to strip out obsolete provisions.

events.title: Passed and given assent
events.description: Parliament cleared the Bill after a select committee review, and it received the President's assent the same month.

events.title: The Act takes effect
events.description: Income earned from this date is governed by the 2025 Act. Tax year 2026-27 is the first year under the new law.

events.title: First Form No. 26 audit reports due
events.description: The tax audit report under section 63 [old 44AB] moves to a single Form No. 26, replacing Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD, due one month before the return.

events.title: First corporate returns under the new Act
events.description: Companies and other audited businesses file their first returns for tax year 2026-27 under section 263 [old 139].

children.text: One Term Replaces Two: The Tax Year

markDefs.definition: The 12 months of the financial year, beginning 1 April, for which income is computed and taxed. It replaces both the previous year and the assessment year of the old law.

, so the same money carried two labels a year apart. Pick the wrong one while paying tax online and the money landed in the wrong year. Section 3 of the new Act collapses both into a single

body.caption: The same twelve months, old language and new

cells: Tax year 2026-27, the first year under the new Act

body.text: Section 536(3) handles the overlap. Where the new Act refers to a tax year, it maps back to the corresponding previous year of the old Act. So an assessment, appeal or notice for income earned up to 31 March 2026 continues under the 1961 Act, with its old section numbers, even while your current year runs under the new one. Expect both numbering systems to appear in your files for the next few years.

body.title: Quick Check: Naming the Year
body.question: Your company earns profit between 1 April 2026 and 31 March 2027. Under the new Act, what is that period called?
body.explanation: It is simply tax year 2026-27, named after the twelve months in which the income was earned. Under the old law the same income would have been previous year 2026-27, assessed in assessment year 2027-28. One label now does the work of two.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The New Vocabulary
body.textWithBlank: The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces both previous year and assessment year with a single concept called the ___.
body.explanation: Section 3 defines the tax year as the twelve months of the financial year starting 1 April. Every deadline, rate and filing now hangs off that one label.

children.text: What Changed and What Did Not

columns.label: Changed
points: Every section number, and the chapter each rule sits in
Previous year and assessment year, now a single tax year
Long prose provisos replaced by 57 tables and 46 formulae
TDS provisions consolidated into one section with tables, instead of dozens of separate sections
The tax audit report, now a single Form No. 26
Obsolete provisions that had stopped applying years ago, now removed

columns.label: Did not change
points: Tax rates, slabs, surcharge and cess, which are set by the Finance Act each year
The 22% concessional corporate regime and the choice it demands
TDS rates and thresholds on your payments
How capital gains, business income and salary are computed
Tax audit thresholds, and the basic filing calendar
Your obligation for earlier years, which stays with the 1961 Act

body.text: This is the trap for the next few years. Almost every article, template, invoice format, payroll setup and accounting software field you already have quotes 1961 section numbers. Searching online for a rule will still mostly surface old numbering. Do not assume a blog post is out of date because it says 194J, and do not assume it is current either. Check the mapping before you rely on it.

children.text: The Section Numbers a Business Owner Will Actually Use

You do not need all 536 sections. For most businesses, the working set is about a dozen, and the rest of this course uses them throughout. Each is shown here in the new numbering, with the old number in brackets.

cells: Expenses that cannot be deducted, including partner remuneration limits in 35(e)
Presumptive taxation on a percentage of turnover
Books of account you must maintain
Tax audit, reported in Form No. 26
The default personal regime and its slabs
Minimum alternate tax and alternate minimum tax, now in one place
Filing your return, including belated, revised and updated returns
TDS on your payments, arranged as tables

body.label: Dozens of TDS sections, now one
body.context: Payments to contractors, professionals, partners and shareholders sit in tables inside a single section. Payments to partners, for example, are Table for Payments to Any Person, serial 7, carrying forward old section 194T.

children.text: Section 263 now holds every kind of return in one place: the original return, the belated one, the revised one and the updated one. Two deadlines inside it are worth memorising. A belated return is allowed within nine months from the end of the tax year. A revised return gets twelve months from the end of the tax year, three months more than the old law allowed.

cells: Within 9 months from the end of the tax year
Within 12 months from the end of the tax year

body.text: Filing dates move. The due date for non-audit business filers was pushed from 31 July to 31 August by the Finance Act, 2026, and the CBDT has extended dates mid-year before. Confirm each date on the income tax portal for the year you are actually filing, rather than trusting any printed calendar, including this one.

body.title: Scenario: The Payroll Software Nobody Updated
body.scenario: A 60-person logistics company in Nagpur runs payroll and vendor payments on software configured years ago. Its vendor agreements say TDS will be deducted under section 194C, its offer letters mention section 192, and its finance executive files returns using the labels she has always used. It is now May 2026, and the first month of tax year 2026-27 is closing.
body.prompt: What actually needs to change, and what does not?
body.modelAnswer: The obligations themselves are unchanged. The company still deducts TDS on contractor payments and on salaries, at the same rates and thresholds, and deposits it on the same dates. What changes is where those rules live: contractor and salary deductions now sit inside section 393 of the 2025 Act, in its tables, rather than in separate sections 194C and 192. Practically, the finance team should confirm with the software vendor that challans, payment codes and TDS return formats are updated for the new Act, refresh contract and offer letter templates to reference the new provisions, and brief the team that a notice quoting an unfamiliar section number is not necessarily wrong. Two dates should go into the calendar now: Form No. 26 by 30 September 2027 and the return by 31 October 2027 for this tax year, if the company is audited. Any open assessment or notice for income up to 31 March 2026 still runs under the 1961 Act, so old section references in those files are correct and should not be changed.

body.title: Try It: How Much Shorter Is the New Law?
body.prompt: The 1961 Act ran to roughly 5.12 lakh words. The 2025 Act runs to roughly 2.6 lakh. By approximately what percentage did the word count fall?
body.explanation: (5.12 minus 2.6) divided by 5.12 is about 0.492, or roughly 49%. Sections fell from 819 to 536 and chapters from 47 to 23 over the same rewrite. The length came down because obsolete provisions were dropped and prose was replaced with tables.

body.title: Transition Checklist for Your Business
steps: Ask your accounting and payroll vendors, in writing, to confirm their systems are updated for the 2025 Act
Update contract, invoice and offer letter templates that quote 1961 section numbers
Put Form No. 26 and the return due date for the current tax year into a shared calendar, not one person's head
Keep files for income up to 31 March 2026 under old section references, since those proceedings continue under the 1961 Act
Brief whoever opens the post or the e-filing portal that section numbers on notices will look unfamiliar
Re-verify due dates on the income tax portal each year, because they move

cards.definition: The twelve months of the financial year beginning 1 April, for which income is computed and taxed. Defined in section 3, it replaces both previous year and assessment year.
The transition rule mapping a tax year under the new Act to the corresponding previous year under the 1961 Act, so old proceedings continue undisturbed.
The single tax audit report form under section 63 [old 44AB], replacing Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD for tax years from 1 April 2026.
The single section covering original, belated, revised and updated returns, including their due dates.
One consolidated TDS section, with tables listing each kind of payment, its threshold and its rate.
The annual Budget law that sets rates, slabs, surcharge and cess. The Income-tax Act sets the rules, the Finance Act sets the numbers.

points: The Income-tax Act, 2025 governs income from 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act with 536 sections across 23 chapters
Rates, slabs, thresholds and the way income is computed did not change, because those come from the Finance Act each year
Previous year and assessment year are gone, replaced by a single tax year defined in section 3
Section 536(3) keeps earlier years running under the old Act, so both numbering systems will coexist in your files for a while
Most businesses need about a dozen sections, notably 200, 202, 206, 263, 393, 63, 62, 58 and 35
The practical work of the transition is unglamorous: update templates, brief your software vendors, and reconfirm filing dates each year

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Due dates and forms change through notifications and each year's Finance Act. Verify current requirements on the income tax portal or with a qualified chartered accountant before filing.
